Between 1514Z and 1934Z on 6 May, the aircraft's full-motion video sensor observed five unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), with the first characterized as possibly resembling a missile and the remaining four assessed as likely birds. 36.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting a reconnaissance flight over Iraq on May 20–21, 2022, during Operation Inherent Resolve. Aircraft callsign 1.4a conducted a 18-hour 54-minute ISR mission supporting Operation Phantom Flex, collecting signals intelligence via Airhandler Version 2. At 20:43Z on May 20, the crew observed one unidentified aircraft (UAP) flying north to northeast; the screener could not achieve positive identification before the object moved out of range. The report documents the sighting but provides no determination of the UAP's origin or nature.

37.tldr: This is a declassified Air Force mission report documenting a 20.5-hour ISR surveillance flight over Syria on 29–30 May 2022. The aircraft conducted target development and signals collection on Syrian naval operations, coastal defense sites, and military facilities in the Eastern Mediterranean. At 2147Z on 29 May, the asset was intercepted by 1–3 Russian SU-30 fighters that approached to approximately 5 nautical miles before departing westward with no mission impact. At 0117Z on 30 May, one small UAP was observed flying north-northeast; the screener could not obtain a positive identification.

38.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an armed reconnaissance flight over Syria on July 31, 2022. The aircraft, callsign redacted, conducted 20+ hours of imagery and signals intelligence collection in support of Task Force Chosin under Operation Inherent Resolve, tracking military activity including vehicles, personnel, and equipment at multiple locations. At 02:39 UTC on July 31, the crew observed an unidentified aerial phenomenon lasting less than one minute near grid square 37SFU271, moving north to south; the report provides no further description of the UAP event and does not state a conclusion.
quotes: AT 310239Z, [AIRCRAFT] OBSERVED AN UAP EVENT IVO 37SFU2[GRID]. THE UAP OCCURED IN LESS THAN A MINUTE, WITH THE UAP MOVING FROM N TO S.
COORDINATION WAS SATISFACTORY DUE TO QUALITY OF PRODUCTS.
FROM 05212 TO 07152, [AIRCRAFT] FOLLOWED THE VEHICLES AND OBSERVED 2X STOPS IVO 37SFU2[GRID].
AREA ASSESSED TO BE A POSS SHOOTING RANGE.
key_facts: Mission date: July 31, 2022 (301822Z to 311529Z)
Location: Syria, grid squares 37SFU (multiple); UAP observed at 37SFU271

UAP event: July 31, 02:39 UTC, duration <1 minute, trajectory north to south
Supported unit: Task Force Chosin; operation: Inherent Resolve

39.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an ISR flight over Iraq on December 1–2, 2022. At 1620Z on December 1, the aircrew observed one possible UAP/UAV flying west to east near grid 38S MB 4~83 while conducting routine intelligence collection. The crew did not pursue the object and continued their tasked mission; no further events were reported. The sighting remained unresolved with no physical description, signatures, or technical parameters recorded.

40.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report documenting a Defensive Counter-Air (DCA) flight by two F-15E Strike Eagles from Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Iraq, on February 21, 2023, in support of Operation Inherent Resolve. During the mission near Shaddadi, Syria, the aircrew reported observing three possible unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) at Flight Level 240 with no radar returns, and separately sighted one possible balloon at FL210; both sightings were documented via weapon system video. The flight also experienced radar jamming from a suspected Turkish X-band jammer north of Shaddadi. The crew experienced no health effects and the observations remain unresolved with no further tactical report (NFTR) issued.

OBS lX POSS BALLOON IVO SHADDADI AT FL210. WSV PRODUCED. NFTR.

41.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting a Defensive Counter Air (DCA) patrol flown by two F-16CM fighters from Prince Sultan Air Base, Iraq on March 31, 2023 during Operation Inherent Resolve. At 2302 UTC on March 31, the flight observed multiple bright objects maneuvering rapidly west to east northeast of the restricted landing zone at FL600+. The objects were intermittently captured on targeting pod TV mode for approximately 20 seconds before becoming dim and disappearing; none were observed in formation patterns seen in prior sorties. An analyst compared targeting pod imagery of the possible UAPs against star returns and found the results were different, but no conclusion is stated.
quotes: STARTING AT 2302:052 FLT OBSERVED SEVERAL BRIGHT OBJECTS MANUEVERING QUICKLY WEST TO EAST NE OF RLZ
FLT WOULD OBTAIN POSS UAP ON TARGETING POD (TV MODE) FOR APPROX 20S BEFORE OBJECT WOULD BECOME DIM AND DISAPPEAR
NONE OF THE OBJECTS WERE SEEN IN ANY FORMATIONS AS PREVIOUSLY SEEN IN PRIOR SORTIES
FLT COMPARED TARGETING POD BETWEEN POSS UAP AND STAR. RESULTS WERE DIFFERENT
key_facts: Incident date: March 31, 2023, 2302 UTC
Location: Northeast of restricted landing zone (RLZ), Iraq, Operation Inherent Resolve
Aircraft: 2-ship F-16CM fighters, 77th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron, Prince Sultan Air Base (OEPS)
Observation altitude: FL265 (friendly aircraft); FL600+ (UAP)
Sensor: Targeting pod (SNIPER LDP) in TV mode; ALR-56M Radar Warning Receiver
Objects observed: Possibly 10–20 bright objects maneuvering west to east; captured on targeting pod ~20 seconds before dimming and disappearing

42.tldr: This is a USCENTCOM Mission Report (MISREP) documenting a Joint Surveillance and Reconnaissance (JSR) flight by the 50th Attack Squadron on 31 October 2023 in the Arabian Gulf near the UAE. The aircraft operated under Operation Spartan Shield for approximately 17 hours on station, during which the pilot received a professional radio call from Iranian Air Defense requesting safe distance from the border and observed two unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) at different times. Both UAP were assessed as benign, showed no maneuverability or response to observer actions, and were neither engaged nor reported as posing a threat; no physical characteristics, propulsion, or advanced capabilities could be determined from the limited sensor data.

43.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting a Joint Surveillance and Reconnaissance (JSR) flight by the 50th Attack Squadron over the Arabian Gulf on October 31, 2023. The aircraft conducted a 20-hour 43-minute mission from Al Dhafra (OMAM) in support of Operation Spartan Shield and Naval Forces Central Command. At 0241Z and 0322Z on October 31, the pilot reported two unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) sightings at approximately 39RXK6 coordinates while flying at FL243 and 162 KTAS. The first UAP displayed thermal signatures showing cold readings and was traveling at an estimated 320 MPH; the second was moving at approximately 440 MPH. Both observations were assessed as benign with no intelligent control detected. The mission intelligence products were exploited by DGS-2 upon landing.

44.tldr: This is a declassified Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an ISR flight over the Mediterranean Sea on 25 January 2024. At 0509Z, the crew of an aircraft operating from LGLR observed a single unidentified aerial phenomenon while in transit at FL250. The UAP appeared diamond-shaped with a non-maneuvering probe attachment, visible only on SWIR camera, traveling at approximately 434 knots for roughly 2 minutes before the sighting ended without incident. The observer assessment classified the phenomenon as benign, with no anomalous response to the aircraft's presence and no effects on personnel or equipment.
quotes: THE UAP APPEARED DIAMOND IN SHAPE WITH A NON-MANUEVERING PROBE AT THE BOTTOM. THE UAP ONLY APPEARED ON THE SWIR CAMERA.
THE EVENT LASTED APPROX 2 MINUTES ENDING AT 0511Z, WITHOUT ANY OTHER INCIDENT OCCURING.
UPON INITIAL OBSERVATION, THE UAP WAS FLYING AT A SPEED OF APPROX 434 KNOTS.
Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign
key_facts: Mission date: 25 January 2024
UAP initial contact: 0509Z, lasted approximately 2 minutes (0509Z–0511Z)
Location: Mediterranean Sea, coordinates 35SQT44/35SPT63 (estimated), FL200–FL250 altitude
Aircraft: Single ISR asset, callsign and tail number redacted, departed LGLR at 0109Z
UAP description: Diamond-shaped with non-maneuvering tail probe, visible only on SWIR sensor, traveling ~434 knots
Observer: Senior Airman/E-4, 56 SOIS; assessment: benign, no intelligent control confirmed, no objects recovered

45.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Intelligence Summary and Mission Report (MISREP) documenting an ISR mission over the Gulf of Oman on 6–7 June 2024. During return-to-base at 0457Z on 7 June, the aircrew observed a single unidentified object described as a glowing hot spherical object with a vertical cylindrical pole attached to its bottom, flying at 140 knots just above water level at coordinates near 40RFM60. The observer assessed the object as benign; there was no interrogation, engagement, or reaction from the object. The document contains extensive redactions of aircraft type, tail number, and operational details.

46.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report documenting an armed overwatch flight over Iraq on September 20, 2024, during which the crew observed an unidentified aerial phenomenon. While conducting a weapons calibration at approximately 20:27Z, the aircraft's weapons systems officer and combat systems officer detected an object moving at high speed through their sensor field of view immediately after a munition release. The UAP created an infrared lens flare on the MX-20 and MX-25 targeting pods, indicating a significant heat source, but the crew observed no response to their actions and did not re-observe the object. The agency assessed the sighting as benign with no effects on personnel or equipment.
quotes: UAP FLEW THROUGH (b)(1)1.4a SENSOR IN BETWEEN MUNITION RELEASE AND MUNITION IMPACT
THE UAP CREATED AN IR LENS FLARE ON THE MX-20 & MX-25 SENSORS, INDICATING A SIGNIFICANT HEAT SOURCE. THE UAP MOVED AT A HIGH RATE OF SPEED THROUGH THE SENSOR FIELD OF VIEW.
IT IS UNKNOWN AT THIS TIME WHETHER AN OBJECT DETACHED ITSELF FROM THE PRIMARY UAP IMMEDIATELY BEFORE LEAVING THE SENSOR FIELD OF VIEW.
PATH OF MOVEMENT APPEARED PREDETERMINED AND NOT IN RESPONSE TO (b)(1)1.4a's DETECTION
key_facts: Incident date: September 20, 2024, 20:27Z
Location: Ayn Al Asad Airbase (AAAB) Restricted Operating Zone RAINDROP, Iraq
Observer: Weapons Systems Officer and Combat Systems Officer aboard armed overwatch aircraft
Sensor detection: MX-20 and MX-25 targeting pods; IR signature observed
Aircraft altitude: FL130 (13,000 feet); speed 170 KIAS
Assessment: Benign; no effects on personnel or equipment; no re-observation of UAP

48.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an ISR (intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) operation over Syria on October 20–21, 2024, flown by a single aircraft from Oman. Between 1559Z and 1644Z on October 20, the aircrew observed multiple light/glare phenomena of unknown origin crossing the full-motion video (FMV) camera feed at various angles, described as a misshapen, uneven ball of white light; the crew assessed the phenomenon as benign with no mission impact and ruled out a lasing event. The observation was recorded and exploited by the Ground Exploitation Team. The three-part ISR mission lasted 20 hours 24 minutes total, with 14 hours 22 minutes on station and primary focus on target development related to violent extremist groups (VEO) in support of Operation Inherent Resolve.

AIRCREW CONSIDERED THIS NO MISSION IMPACT OR CHANGE AND UAP WAS BENIGN.
LIGHT/GLARE FROM UNKNOWN ORIGIN FLASHED ACCROSS FMV CAMERA FEED. AIRCREW ASSESSED THIS NOT TO BE A LASING EVENT.

49.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) mission report documenting a 20-hour operational flight over Syria on October 20–21, 2024. During the second tasking segment (1230–2318Z on October 20), the aircrew observed multiple light/glare phenomena of unknown origin crossing the full-motion video (FMV) camera feed at five separate times between 1559Z and 1644Z. The phenomenon was described as a misshapen, uneven ball of white light with halo effects. The aircrew assessed the observation as benign with no mission impact and ruled out hostile intent or lasing. The event was cataloged as a UAP incident and formally reported to DoD.
quotes: MISHAPEN AND UNEVEN BALL OF WHITE LIGHT.
FROM 1559Z-1644Z, OBSERVED MULTIPLE GLARES OR LIGHT FROM UNKNOWN ORIGIN AT DIFFERENT ANGLES AND DIRECTIONS.
AIRCREW CONSIDERED THIS NO MISSION IMPACT OR CHANGE AND UAP WAS BENIGN.
AIRCREW ASSESSED THIS NOT TO BE A LASING EVENT.
key_facts: Date of incident: October 20–21, 2024 (October 20, 1559Z–1644Z for UAP observations)
Location: Syria, grid 37S FU 36–81 (primary observation area)
Observer: E-4 aircrew member aboard classified ISR platform, altitude 20,088 ft, airspeed 144 knots
UAP observations: Five separate light/glare events crossing FMV camera feed; no radar interrogation; no intelligent control assessed
Assessment: Benign, no lasing detected, no effects on personnel or equipment, no materials recovered
Unit: 12th Special Operations Squadron (12 SOS), 27th Special Operations Wing (27 SOW), USCENTCOM

50.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force intelligence mission report (MISREP) documenting a 20-hour ISR sortie over Syria on 20–21 October 2024. During the mission, the aircrew observed multiple unidentified light phenomena between 1559Z and 1644Z on 20 October while conducting full-motion video collection at approximately 20,088 feet. The UAP was described as a misshapen ball of white light that flashed across the camera feed at different angles; the aircrew assessed it as benign with no mission impact and found no evidence of intelligent control or lasing activity.

51.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an intelligence surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) flight over the Aegean Sea on 27 October 2023. During the mission, the aircrew observed one unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) flying just above the ocean surface, executing multiple sharp 90-degree turns at an estimated 80 mph before disappearing from sensor feed at 0038Z. The object was described as seemingly circular and too small to discern details; the observer assessed it as benign, no intelligent control was attributed to it, and no advanced capabilities were identified. The aircraft maintained full motion video collection capability throughout the encounter.

53.tldr: This is a Range Fouler Debrief Form, a U.S. military incident report documenting a UAP sighting during an ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance) mission in the Arabian Gulf on May 14, 2020 at 20:40 UTC. A single solid white object was observed flying through the sensor field of view, exhibiting erratic movements above water; the crew maintained intermittent visual tracking at 4x zoom before losing track due to poor sensor placement. The document remains unresolved regarding the object's identity or propulsion.
quotes: a solid white object flew through the FOV. There was a temporarily lose of the object but re-acquired shortly thereafter.
crew was able to follow the object as it appeared to make erratic moments above the water.
During the follow, crew was able to obtain 4x zoom on the object but lost the object due to poor track place ent.
the sensor operator was continuously manipulating the sensor to maintain eyes on the object.
key_facts: Incident date: 05/14/20, time 20:40:00 UTC
Location: Arabian Gulf, contact working area W-28314, coordinates 28°N 49°E
Contact altitude: 20,000 feet (constant), wind direction at contact altitude not specified

56.tldr: This is a military incident report form documenting a UAP detection by aircrew in the Arabian Sea on October 15, 2020. At 14:18:39 UTC, personnel flying at 19,073 feet over the Gulf of Aden tracked a round, cold object via infrared sensor traveling at 20 mph, approximately 4.06 nautical miles away. The object displayed abrupt directional changes during the one-minute contact and appeared as bright white on a black-hot IR setting. The report provides sensor parameters, location data in MGRS format, and requests supporting video files be archived.
quotes: While at 19,073 HAT over the Gulf of Aden we tracked a round, cold object in IR traveling 3,19 degrees at 20 mph.
It made a few abrupt directional changes during the 1 minute contact.
Our sensor was aimed -50 degrees below our altitude with a slant range of 4.06NM and ground range of 4.78KM. The IR sensor was set to black hot and the object in question was a bright white.

57.tldr: This is a technical research report prepared by the Research Triangle Institute for the U.S. Air Force Space Command, dated September 10, 1996, documenting methodology for modeling unlikely space-launch vehicle failures in risk calculations. The report addresses Mode-5 failure responses—rare malfunctions causing vehicles to deviate significantly from intended flight paths—and establishes shaping constants for the impact-density function used in the DAMP (facility DAMage and Personnel injury) risk-analysis program. The report analyzes failure histories of Atlas, Delta, and Titan launch vehicles from their program origins through August 1996, deriving failure probabilities and response-mode distributions to support launch-area safety assessments.
quotes: Although Mode-5 failure responses are much less likely to occur than those that result in impacts near the flight line, risk-analysis studies are incomplete without them.

Less likely malfunctions may cause a vehicle to execute a sustained turn away from the flight line. Examples are control failures that cause the rocket engine to lock in a fixed position near null, or failures leading to erroneous orientation of the guidance platform.

The probability that the center of the secondary function lies in some region or on some building (population center) is determined by integrating the primary impact-density function for the class over the region or building.

An appendix to the report contains a listing and brief narrative failure history of the Atlas, Delta, and Titan missile and space-vehicle launches from the Eastern and Western Ranges from the beginning of each program through August 1996.

 1. Introduction
The debris from most launch vehicles that fail catastrophically tend to impact close to the
intended flight line. Typical failures that produce such results are premature thrust
termination, stage ignition failure, tank rupture or explosion, or rapid out-of-control
tumble. Less likely malfunctions may cause a vehicle to execute a sustained turn away
from the flight line. Examples are control failures that cause the rocket engine to lock in a
fixed position near null, or failures leading to erroneous orientation of the guidance
platform. Such failures should not be ignored, since they may produce nearly all or a
significant part of the risks to population centers that are more than a mile or so uprange or
many miles away from the flight line. Consequently, RTI has been tasked to estimate the
probabilities of occurrence of these less-likely failures, and to determine optimum values
for the shaping constants of the associated impact-density function

RTI has developed a prototype risk-analysis program (1) to analyze the level of risk in the
launch area when ballistic missiles and space vehicles are launched, and (2) to provide
guidelines for launch operations and launch-area risk management. This program, "facility
DAMage and Personnel injury" (DAMP), uses information about the launch vehicle, its
trajectory and failure responses, and facilities and populations in the launch area to estimate
hit probabilities and casualty expectations. When a missile or space vehicle malfunctions,
people and facilities may be subjected to significant risks from falling inert debris, or from
overpressures and secondary debris produced by a stage, component, or large propellant
chunk that explodes on impact. Although fire, toxic materials, and radiation may also
subject personnel to significant danger, these hazards are not addressed in program DAMP.
Hazards are greatest in the launch area and along the intended flight line, but lesser
hazards exist throughout the area inside the impact limit lines. Small hazards exist even
outside these lines if the flight termination system fails or other unlikely events occur.

In computing launch-area risks, DAMP makes no attempt to model vehicle failures per
se. A list of possible failures for any vehicle would be extensive, and variations in
failures from vehicle to vehicle would complicate the modeling process. Instead,
DAMP models failure responses. Regardless of the exact nature of the failures that can
occur, there are only six possible response modes that affect risks on the ground, five
for failure responses, and one to model the behavior of a normal vehicle. The six
modes are described in Appendix A. It can be seen from the descriptions that impacts
resulting from failure-response Modes 1, 2, and 3 occur at most a mile or two from the
launch point, while those from Mode 4 can only occur near the flight line, even though the
vehicle may tumble before breakup or destruct. Although the hazards outside the launch
area and away from the flight line may be small, vehicle flight tests through the years have
demonstrated that finite hazards do exist in these areas. Such hazards are due almost
entirely to Mode-5 failure responses, even through the probability of a Mode-5 failure may
be only a small part of the total failure probability. The Mode-5 failure-response,
theoretical though it is, was developed to reflect the facts that: (1) unlikely vehicle failures



9/10/96                                        1                                            RTI
 can cause impacts uprange or well away from the intended flight line, and (2) some vehicle
failures cannot logically be classified as Response Modes 1, 2, 3, or 4.

In- keeping with the above, the Mode-5 impact-density function was developed with the
characteristics listed below. The function, which fills the void left by Modes 1 through 4, is
sufficiently robust to include all possible impacts, yet seemingly comports with observed
test results.

(1)   Impacts can occur in any direction from the launch point and at any range within
      the vehicle's energy capabilities.

(2)   At any given impact range from the launch point, the likelihood of impact
      decreases as the angular deviation from the flight line increases, becoming least.
      likely in the uprange direction. For any fixed angular deviation from the flight
      line, the likelihood of impact decreases as the impact range increases.

(3)   At fixed impact ranges near the launch point, the impact density function changes
      gradually as the impact direction swings 180° from downrange to uprange. As
      the impact range increases, the decrease in the density function becomes
      progressively more and more rapid with change in impact direction. In other
      words, the greater the impact range, the more rapidly the density function
      changes with angular deviation from the flight line.                              •

As modeled in DAMP, the effects of destruct action on the Mode-5 density function are
accounted for in the launch area by supplementing impacts inside the impact limit lines
with those that would occur outside the impact limit lines if no destruct action were taken.
 The Mode-5 failure-response methodology was fully developed in an earlier RTI report111•
 As pointed ·out there, the shape of the impact density function can be controlled somewhat
 through the selection of shaping constants that appear in the defining equation Intuition
 suggests that the constants should be vehicle dependent, since (1) ruggedly built missiles
 would, after a malfunction, be more likely to impact well away from the flight line than
 would a fragile space vehicle that tends to break up before deviating significantly; and
.(2) certain vehicles, after a malfunction, tend to stabilize and •continue thrusting at large
 angles of attack, while other vehicles that experience similar malfunctions tend to tumble.
 Hit probabilities computed by-program DAMP for targets located more than two miles or
 so uprange from the pad or more than a few miles from the flight line, are due almost
 entirely to the Mode-5 impact-density function Thus, the assumed probability of
 occurrence of a Mode-5 response as well as the selected Mode-5 constants are of
 considerable importance.

The tasking for this. study is set _forth as Task No. 10/95-77, Paragraph 2.0, of Contract
FO4703-91-C-0112. The primary purpose of the tasking is: "Perform a study to
determine the best values for Mode-5 failure probability and the Mode-5 density-
function shaping constant A." Although not explicitly included in the statement of work,
the study also develops absolute failure probabilities for Atlas, Delta, and Titan, and

9/10/%                                        2                                           RTI
 relative probabilities of occurrence for all failure-response modes for these vehicles, LLVl,
and other new launch systems.

Although it may be reasonable to establish the relative probability of occurrence of a
Mode-5 failure response by empirical means, the number of Mode-5 failures is too small to
have any hope of establishing accurate values for the shaping constants from this sample
alone. Inadequate descriptions of vehicle behavior in the available historical records and
uncertainty in impact location following a malfunction add to the difficulty of classifying
failure responses. In view of the limited data available for vehicles that have experienced
Mode-5 failures, the values chosen for the Mode-5 constants must depend on simulations of
vehicle behavior following failure.

2. Examples Showing Need for Mode 5
The need for a Mode-5 response or some similar response mode (or a multiplicity of other
response modes) can be seen from the following vehicle performance descriptions extracted
from Appendix D:

(1)   Atlas BE, 24 Jan 61. Missile stability was lost at about 161 seconds, some 30
      seconds after BECO, probably due to failure of the servo-amplifier power supply.
      The sustainer engine shut down at 248 seconds, and the vernier engines about 10
      seconds later. Impact occurred 1316 miles downrange and 215 miles crossrange. •

(2)   Titan M-4, 6 Oct 61. A one-bit error in the W velocity accumulation caused impact
      86 miles short and 14 miles right of target.
(3)   Atlas 145D (Mariner R-1), 22 July 62. Booster stage and flight appeared normal
      until after booster staging at guidance enable at about 157 seconds. Operation of
      guidance rate beacon was intermittent. Due to this and faulty guidance equations,
      erroneous guidance commands were given based on invalid rate data. Vehicle
      deviations became evident at 172 seconds and continued throughout flight with a
      maximum yaw deviation of 60° and pitch deviation of 28° occurring at 270
      seconds. The vehicle deviated grossly from the planned trajectory in azimuth and
      velocity, and executed abnormal maneuvers in pitch and yaw. The missile was
      destroyed by the RSO at 293.5 seconds, some 12 seconds after SECO.
(4)   Atlas SLV-3 (GTA-9), 17 May 66. Vehicle became unstable when B2 pitch control
      was lost at 121 seconds. Loss of pitch control resulted in a pitch-down maneuver
      much greater than 90°. Guidance control was lost at 132 seconds. After BECO,
      the vehicle stabilized in an abnormal attitude. Although the vehicle did not
      follow the planned trajectory, SECO (at 280 seconds), VECO (at 298 seconds), and
      Agena separation occurred normally from programmer commands.

(5)   Atlas 95F (ABRES/AFSC), 3 May 68. Immediately after liftoff the telemetered roll
      and yaw rates indicated that the missile was erratic. During the first 10 seconds of
      flight the missile yawed hard to the left. It then began a hard yaw to the right,

9/10/96                                      3                                           RTI
       crossed over the flight line and continued toward the right destruct line. Shortly
      thereafter the missile apparently pitched up violently and the HP began moving
      back toward the beach. The missile was destructed at about 45 seconds when the
      altitude was about 14,000 feet and the downrange distance about 9 miles. Major
      pieces impacted less than a mile offshore, indicating uprange movement of the
      impact point during the last part of thrusting flight.
(6)   Delta Intelsat III, 18 Sep·68. Due to loss of rate gyro, undamped pitch oscillations
      began at 20 seconds. A series of violent maneuvers followed at 59 seconds.
      During the 13-second period while these maneuvers continued, the vehicle
      pitched down some 270°, then up 210°, and then made a large yaw to the left. At
      72 seconds the vehicle regained control and flew stably in a down and leftward
      direction until 100 seconds. At this time, with the main engine against the pitch
      and yaw stops, the destabilizing aerodynamic forces became so· large that quasi-
      control could no longer be maintained. The first stage broke up at 103 seconds.
      The second stage was destroyed by the RSO at 110.6 seconds. Major pieces
      impacted about 12 miles downrange and 2 miles left of the flight line.
(7)   Delta Pioneer E, 27 Aug 69. First-stage hydraulics system failed a few seconds
      before first-~tage burnout (MECO). The vehicle pitched down, yawed left, rolled
      counterclockwise driving all gyros off limits, and then tumbled. Second-stage
      separation and ignition occurred while the vehicle was out of control. After about
      20 seconds, the second stage regained control in a yaw-right, pitch-up attitude. It
      flew stably in this attitude for about 240 seconds until destroyed by the safety
      officer at T+484 seconds.
(8)   Atlas 68E, 8 Dec 80. Flight appeared normal until 102.7 seconds when the lube oil
      pressure on the B2 booster engine suddenly dropped. At 120.1 seconds, the
      engine shut down, followed 385 msec later by guidance shutdown of the Bl
      engine. The asymmetric thrust during shutdown caused yaw and roll rates that
      the flight-control system could not correct. As a result, attitude control was lost
      and the thrusting sustainer pivoted the missile to a retrofire attitude before the
      vehicle could be stabilized: After the booster package was jettisoned, the missile
      was stabilized and decelerating in the retrofire mode by 148 seconds. The
      sustainer continued thrusting in this attitude until 282.9 seconds when reentry
      heating apparently caused sustainer shutdown and vehicle.breakup.

possible location for the :MPI for each debris class. On the other hand, the Mod~S impact-
density function for each debris class consists of a primary part and a secondary

61.tldr: This is an email chain documenting a derivative classification review for an Intelligence Information Report (IIR) concerning a civilian UAP sighting. On the night of March 2023 in the Pacific Time Zone, a civilian observer reported an eight-minute sighting of a large blue triangular object emitting whitish-blue light from multiple points, hovering near a national security facility for approximately three minutes before moving upward in jerking or jumping motions inconsistent with conventional jet propulsion. The reporter could not identify the object's means of control or propulsion, nor determine front or rear orientation, and did not believe it was a drone. The Department of War approved reclassification of the summary to UNCLASSIFIED level.
quotes: a large blue featureless triangular object with a solid, unwavering silhouette emitting powerful "whitish blue" light from multiple points along its perimeter
hovering" stationary above or near a national security facility for approximately three minutes
move to a position higher in their field of view...characterized the object's motion as "backing up" in a "jerking" or "jumping" manner inconsistent with "smooth" jet propulsion
could not discern whether or how the object was controlled, could not identify its means of propulsion, and could not determine whether it had a defined "front or rear"

Location: Pacific Time Zone, near a national security facility
Duration of observation: approximately 8 minutes
Object shape: large triangular; color: blue; featureless markings
Motion: stationary hover (3 min), then jerking/jumping upward movement
Reporter type: civilian; obtained via personal cellular device

64.tldr: This is a U.S. Navy mission report documenting a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft observation of an unidentified low-flying object near Latakia, Syria on November 18, 2016. At approximately 1310Z, the P-8 detected via EO/IR sensor what was characterized as a possible missile in sea-skim mode traveling at roughly 500 knots on a southeasterly heading, originating from an unknown location near a Russian naval vessel. The object was tracked for approximately 2 minutes before visual contact was lost around 40 nm northwest of Latakia. The mission commander assessed the interaction as safe and concluded the activity was consistent with standard operations of the Russian naval task group.
quotes: P-IA observed an unidentified low-flying object 86 nm northwest of Latakia from an unknown origin, traveling at approx 500KTS on a southeasterly heading outbound from KCTG, for ~2 minutes.
The possible missile appeared to be in sea skim mode traveling at approximately 500KTS on a southeasterly heading outbound from KCTG.
P-8 lost visual of the object IVO approx. 40 NM northwest of Latakia. The missile was observed to pass between (RUS) INGUL ARS and 1x U/I vessel.
The mission commander for P-8 characterized the interaction as safe.

65.tldr: This is a Range Fouler Debrief form completed by a U.S. Navy pilot (O-3, IHSM-73 squadron) documenting a sighting of three unidentified air contacts in the North Arabian Sea on August 24, 2020 at 00:04:30Z during routine operations. The pilot observed one contact visually, lost it behind a cloud, then regained sight and identified two additional contacts due east of the initial position. All three contacts maintained consistent relative course, speed, and altitude; no radar track, IFF identification, or electronic signature was detected. No interaction occurred and the conclusion remains unresolved.

66.tldr: This is a Range Fouler Reporting Form—a U.S. Department of War incident report documenting an airborne sensor contact over the Gulf of Aden on September 4, 2020. An ISR aircrew at 23,819 feet altitude tracked a round, cold object via infrared sensor traveling at 277 mph on a heading of 168 degrees for 8 minutes, during which it made abrupt directional changes. The object appeared as bright white in black-hot IR mode against a background of 6.1 nautical miles slant range. No radar lock, electronic warfare indications, or identification was achieved. The report does not record a conclusion regarding the object's origin or nature.
quotes: While at 23,819 HAT over the Gulf of Aden we tracked a round, cold object in IR traveling 168 degrees at 277 mph. It made a few abrupt directional changes during the 8 minute contact.
Our sensor was aimed -39 degrees below our altitude with a slant range of 6.1 NM and ground range of 8.81 KM. The IR sensor was set to black hot and the object in question was a bright white.
Contact at 21:09z to 21:17z 04SEP2020.

67.tldr: This is a U.S. Department of War debrief form documenting a Range Fouler incident on October 27, 2020, at 01:12:21Z. A pilot achieved radar lock and target pod video on two unknown contacts at 26,000 feet altitude, unable to close within 16.9 nautical miles for positive identification. The pod showed two infrared-significant contacts with one circling the other in 1/130th of a second before both disappeared; visual tally was confirmed as two red blinking strobes. The pilot reported receiving noise jamming indicated by two chevrons. The incident remained unresolved.

70.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an aerial reconnaissance mission over the Arabian Gulf on August 26–27, 2020, by an aircraft equipped with ANDAS4 targeting pod and AH_GMESH avionics. At 1527Z on August 27, the aircraft observed a formation of unidentified flying objects traveling northeast-northwest along the coast near grid 39RVM8 for approximately 2 minutes before losing visual contact in cloud cover; the aircrew was unable to reacquire the objects. The report notes that light cloud coverage prevented continuous tracking of the UAP event, and the sighting remained unresolved.

71.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP 4782130) documenting an airborne reconnaissance operation over the Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Gulf on September 16, 2020. The aircraft, tasked by Naval Central Command to characterize Iranian vessel activity and establish pattern-of-life intelligence, experienced two separate electromagnetic interference (EMI) events totaling 38 minutes of lost data link, and at 1732Z observed an unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) at coordinates 39RVM5. The document records three hailing calls from Iranian Air Defense, two instances of complete system impact from unknown EMI sources, and the UAP sighting but provides no conclusion regarding the nature of the observed object.
quotes: AT 1732Z, [REDACTED] OBSERVED A UAP IVO 39RVM5[REDACTED]
AT 1248Z, [REDACTED] EXPERIENCED LOST LINK TO POSSIBLE [REDACTED] REGAINED LINK AT 1259Z. THIS RESULTED IN A MEDIUM IMPACT TO THE MISSION
FROM 0318Z TO 1829Z, [REDACTED] CONDUCTED SCANS IAW THE TARGET DECK IN THE ARABIAN GULF (AG). AT 0930Z [REDACTED] OBSERVED AN IR-HMS LAUNCHER IVO 40RCP [REDACTED] ON ABU MUSA ISLAND.
TYPE OF EMI: UNKNOWN... EMI IMPACT TO SYSTEM: COMPLETE... EMI DURATION: 27 MINUTES
key_facts: Mission date: September 16, 2020 (152302Z to 161958Z)
Location: Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf, and Gulf of Oman
Aircraft: Single-ship AREC (airborne reconnaissance) mission, tasked by NAVCENT
Primary sensor: ANDAS4 targeting pod with FMV (Full Motion Video) capability
UAP observation: 1732Z at coordinates 39RVM5, altitude FL180, airspeed 90 KIAS
EMI events: Two instances of complete system loss of link (11 minutes and 27 minutes); type classified as UNKNOWN

73.tldr: This is a USCENTCOM mission report documenting an Air Force reconnaissance flight over the Arabian Gulf on November 2–3, 2020. The aircraft, supporting naval operations in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, observed two unidentified aerial phenomena (UAPs) via full-motion video at approximately 21:43Z and 21:48Z on November 2. The first UAP was observed at location 39RWK at unknown altitude with a bearing of 080T; the second was observed traveling northwest at the same location minutes later. The report provides no analysis, conclusion, or identification of either sighting.

75.tldr: This is a Department of War mission report documenting a UAP observation in the Arabian Gulf region in 2020. A weapons-quality radar track detected a UAP traveling at 31,000 feet mean sea level in the vicinity of 323 degrees, moving with the winds. The object was visually identified in TFLIR (thermal forward-looking infrared) and resembled a balloon similar to previously reported UAP sightings from the 48th Fighter Wing.

WAS ABLE TO MAKE A NEXT TO SHOOT ON THE TRACK AND VISUALLY ID THE UAP IN THE TFLIR.

76.tldr: This is a USCENTCOM mission report (MISREP 9381202) documenting an Air Force ISR sortie over Syria on 9 November 2023. The aircraft conducted target development operations for Operation Inherent Resolve, observing suspected vehicles of interest (VOI) and persons of interest (POI) associated with violent extremist groups. At 21:53Z while returning to base, the aircrew observed an unidentified aerial phenomenon described as a bouncy ball–shaped object traveling at approximately 424 knots at near co-altitude for seven minutes before passing safely beneath the aircraft and going out of range; the observer assessed it as benign with no threat to the aircraft or crew.
quotes: OBSERVED 1X PROB HC UAP SHAPED AS A BOUNCY BALL COME FROM THE SOUTH AT NEAR CO-ALT. 1.4a OBSERVED THE PROB UAP DROP ALTITUDE AND SAFELY PASS THEIR AIRCRAFT WHILE CONSISTANTLY MAINTAINING ~424KN.
YES, TRAVELED ~424KN CONSISTANTLY FOR AT LEAST 7MINS IN THE SHAPE OF A BOUNCY BALL.
NO EMISSIONS CAME FROM THE PROB UAP, UAP WAS NOT CONSIDERED A THREAT TO THE AIRCRAFT OR PUBLIC SAFETY, AND THE UAP HAD NO EFFECTS ON THE AIRCREW.
AFTER 7MIN OF WATCHING, THE PROB UAP BECAME OUT OF RANGE

77.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting an Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) operation conducted on 14 July 2024 in the Gulf of Aden by the 124th Attack Squadron. During the mission, a single unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) was observed at 05:17 UTC on 14 July at coordinates 38P MT 53, flying on a straight flight path at low altitude. The observer assessed the UAP as benign but noted its speed exceeded the aircraft's flying speed; the UAP was tracked until distance made further observation impossible. The incident was documented with full motion video, though the report contains extensive redactions of operational details, sensor specifications, and personnel information.

An Air Force aircraft equipped with full-motion video sensors observed five unidentified aerial phenomena between 1514Z and 1934Z local time near grid coordinates 38SMC53 in the operational area; the first object exhibited characteristics resembling a missile, while the remaining four fit a profile closer to birds. Dust conditions hindered sensor collection. The observation remains categorized as unresolved in the report.

81.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) mission report documenting a 20.5-hour surveillance flight over Syria and the Eastern Mediterranean on 29–30 May 2022. The aircraft conducted target development and collected signals intelligence on Syrian naval operations, military facilities, and Russian assets. At 0117Z on 30 May, the crew observed one small unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) flying north-northeast; the screener could not achieve positive identification. The report also documents a separate encounter at 2147Z on 29 May when 1–3 Russian SU-30 fighters approached within 5 nautical miles of the aircraft, which the crew did not visually acquire.
quotes: AT 0117Z, [AIRCRAFT] OBSERVED A UAP AT 0117Z FLY NORTH TO NORTH EAST AND FOLLOWED AS LONG AS POSSIBLE. [SCREENER] COULD NOT GET A POSITIVE ID ON THE UAP.

AT 2147Z, [AIRCRAFT] WAS REACTED TO BY 1-3 ACFT, INCLUDING IX POSS RFAF SU-30, THAT GOT APPROXIMATELY 5NM FROM [AIRCRAFT]. THE ACFT APPROACHED WESTWARD FROM THE SYRIAN COAST, FLEW DIRECTLY UNDER [AIRCRAFT] ORBIT (FL190, VS [AIRCRAFT] FL243) FOR APPROXIMATELY 2 MIN.
FROM 1938Z TO 0230Z, [AIRCRAFT] COLLECTED ON 39X TGTS: SYRIAN NAVY OPS AREA... LOOKING FOR RFN SURFACE AND SUBSURFACE ROUTES, MUNITION HANDLING, AND PERSONNEL MOVEMENT.
Number of UAP Sighted: 1; UAP Description: [HEAVILY REDACTED]; Screener could not achieve positive identification on the UAP.
key_facts: Mission date: 29–30 May 2022; takeoff 1355Z 29 May from Sigonella AB (LICZ); landing 1025Z 30 May
Total mission time: 20 hours 30 minutes; on-station time: 14 hours 25 minutes
Aircraft type, tail number, and callsign redacted under FOIA exemption 1.4a/1.4g
UAP sighting: 30 May 0117Z at location 37SBV28, altitude FL240, speed 142 KIAS; described as small, unidentified, flying north-northeast; no positive identification achieved
Reaction encounter: 29 May 2147Z with 1–3 Russian SU-30 fighters at approximately 5 nautical miles, approaching from Syrian coast, no weapons employed, mission continued

ISR tasking: 39 target areas surveilled across Syrian Navy operations, Israeli–Lebanese–Syrian region, Latakia naval monitoring, coastal defense sites, and military facilities; assets included ANDAS4 targeting pod and AH/SAR avionics

82.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Armed Reconnaissance mission report (MISREP) filed by the 89th Attack Squadron on 31 July 2022 during Operation Inherent Resolve in Syria. An unidentified aerial phenomenon was observed at 0239Z on 31 July 2022 near grid 37SFU271 while the aircraft was at 19,359 feet altitude. The UAP event lasted less than one minute and moved from north to south. Full motion video was collected and exploited by the Defense Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, but no further details on physical characteristics, identification, or conclusion are provided in the declassified portion.

83.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) mission report (MISREP) documenting a single unidentified aerial phenomenon observation during a planned ISR operation over Iraq on 1 December 2022. An aircraft operating under Operation Inherent Resolve observed one possible UAP/UAV flying west to east near grid 38SMB4~83 at 1620Z; the pilot did not pursue or further investigate and continued the assigned mission. No signatures, effects, or additional details were recorded, and the sighting remains unresolved in the report.

84.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force mission report (MISREP) documenting a Joint Surveillance and Reconnaissance (JSR) operation conducted on 24 October 2023 by the 50th Attack Squadron in the United Arab Emirates as part of Operation SPARTAN SHIELD. During the approximately 20-hour mission, the crew observed two unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP) on 24 October at 0241Z and 0322Z near the Iran-UAE border, both assessed as benign with no intelligent control and no threat to personnel or equipment. Thermal imaging showed the first UAP as cold, and estimated velocities were 320 MPH and 440 MPH respectively; both sightings remain otherwise unresolved with most technical details listed as unknown.
quotes: AT 02412, [AIRCRAFT] OBSERVED IX UAP IVO 39RXK6[REDACTED]. THERMAL SHOWED COLD
AT 03222, [AIRCRAFT] OBSERVED IX UAP IVO 39RXK6[REDACTED]
Observer Assessment of UAP: Benign. UAP Under Intelligent Control (yes/no): NO
AT 01452, [AIRCRAFT] RECEIVED IX GUARD CALL FROM IRANIAN AIR DEFENSE STATING 'MAINTAIN SAFE DISTANCE FROM BORDER'. CALL WAS PROFESSIONAL.
key_facts: Mission date: 24 October 2023; Takeoff 0015Z from OMAM, landing 2058Z
Aircraft type and tail number redacted (designation 1.4a/1.4g); callsign redacted
Unit: 50th Attack Squadron (50ATKS); Wing: 432 Air Expeditionary Wing
UAP Event 1: 0241Z, location 39RXK6[redacted], altitude FL243, estimated velocity 320 MPH, thermal signature cold
UAP Event 2: 0322Z, same general area, altitude FL243, estimated velocity 440 MPH, signature unknown
Both UAP assessed as benign, no intelligent control, no effects on persons or equipment; Iranian Air Defense challenge at 0145Z reported professional

The aircrew assessed the phenomenon as benign, ruled out a lasing event, and found no mission impact. No follow-up intelligence action was taken; the report was filed and declassified in October 2025.

90.tldr: This is a Department of War classified mission report (MISREP) documenting a 20-hour ISR surveillance flight over Syria on 20–21 October 2024. During the mission, an Air Force asset orbiting at 20,088 feet observed multiple light/glare phenomena crossing its full-motion video camera feed between 1559Z and 1644Z. The aircrew described a misshapen, uneven ball of white light appearing at different angles and directions, with halo effects visible at times; no lasing event was suspected. The observer assessed the phenomenon as benign with no mission impact, and it remained unresolved as to origin or nature.

91.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) mission report (MISREP) documenting a UAP sighting near Greece on 27 October 2023. An aircraft from the 33rd Special Operations Squadron, equipped with full-motion video (FMV) and signals intelligence collection systems, observed a single UAP flying just above ocean surface at approximately 0035Z on 27 October while en route to a tasking location. The object was described as seemingly circular, too small to make out details, and performed multiple sharp 90-degree turns at an estimated 80 mph before disappearing from the aircraft's sensor feed at 0038Z. The observer assessed the UAP as benign; the report indicates no intelligent control was detected and the UAP remained unresolved.

92.tldr: This is a U.S. Air Force intelligence summary report (MISREP 9337873) documenting a UAP incident observed during an ISR mission over Greece on 29 October 2023. At 0811Z, an Air Force aircraft equipped with full-motion video sensors detected a circular object flying just above the ocean surface near the Greek coast; the object was lost from the feed moments later. 93.tldr: This is a military incident report form documenting an unresolved UAP sighting during an ISR (Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance) mission in the Middle East on 14 May 2020 at 20:40 UTC. A crew operating infrared sensors observed a solid white object moving erratically above water at approximately 20,000 feet altitude. The object was initially acquired, lost briefly, then re-acquired; the crew achieved 4x zoom before losing track due to sensor placement issues. The sighting remained unresolved with no definitive identification provided.
quotes: While preforming an ISR tasking (UL TN/Black Hot/Lin), a solid white object flew through the FOV. There was a temporarily lose of the object but re-acquired shortly there after.
The crew was able to follow the object as it appeared to make erratic moments above the water.
While following, the sensor operator was continuously manipulating the sensor to maintain eyes on the object.

139.tldr: This is a transcript of radio communications from the Apollo 12 lunar mission in May 1969. During the mission, astronauts reported observing particles of light and flashes emanating from the lunar module and escaping into space, which they initially suspected might be water boiler droplets but noted traveled at high velocity toward the stars. A later anomaly involved an unexplained display of all 8s on the Lunar Module's AGS (Abort Guidance System) DEDA registers pulsing at regular intervals; Houston mission control attributed this to electromagnetic interference (EMI) observed during testing of similar spacecraft at Bethpage. The transcript also documents routine operational communications regarding rendezvous procedures, battery management, and equipment status.
quotes: When you look out the AOT in the dark quadrant? You can see these lights - particles of light. flashes of light just seem to come from - in this case, I'm looking in quadrant 1 which is the left one. It's coming from behind me, the left, and they're just sailing off in space.
I'm getting an all 8 1 s flash on both the address and the information registers at about one-fifth the brilliance of the normal numbers. And a - It's pulsing every second.
Fredo is here. He and I have both seen that phenomena on your DEDA during testing of most all the spacecrafts up at Bethpage, and it's probably an EMI.
key_facts: Apollo 12 mission, May 1969
Observations made near the Moon during lunar module operations
Particles of light reported escaping lunar module vicinity at high velocity
AGS DEDA register anomaly: all 8s display pulsing at ~1-second intervals
Mission control assessment: electromagnetic interference (EMI), previously observed in ground testing

140.tldr: This is a transcript of air-to-ground voice communications from Apollo 17's lunar orbit and surface operations in December 1972. Astronauts reported observing bright, tumbling fragments near the spacecraft during the S-IVB separation maneuver, initially suspected to be debris (ice, paint, or SLA panels). Later observations documented a distant bright object exhibiting rhythmic two-tone flashing at approximately 10–12 Earth diameters away, which the crew and mission control tentatively attributed to the S-IVB booster. A separate incident notes a flash observed on the lunar surface north of Grimaldi crater, which mission control indicated might register on seismometers.
quotes: There's a whole bunch of big ones on my window down there - just bright. It looks like the Fourth of July out of Ron's window.
It is a bright object, and it's obviously rotating because it's flashing...it's way out in the distance...it's definitely not a particle that's nearby.
One unique thing about it, Bob, is that it's got two flashes. As it comes around in rhythmic fashion, you get a very bright flash; and then you get a dull flash.
Hey, I just saw a flash on the lunar surface! It was just out there north of Grimaldi.

Location: Lunar orbit and lunar surface near Grimaldi crater
Bright tumbling fragments observed during S-IVB separation maneuver at 00:03:34–00:03:42 GET
Distant flashing object observed at ~10–12 Earth diameters, exhibiting alternating bright and dull flashes in rhythmic pattern
Lunar surface flash observed north of Grimaldi crater; crew suggested checking seismometers for impact signature
All phenomena tentatively attributed to spacecraft hardware (S-IVB booster, debris, SLA panels) by crew and mission control

142.tldr: This is a NASA crew debriefing document from the Apollo 17 mission dated January 8, 1973, prepared by the Planetary and Earth Sciences Division at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. The extracted text consists of scientific discussion by a speaker identified as Henry regarding ultraviolet and X-ray observations made during the mission, including findings on galactic radiation, the Coma cluster, Lyman-alpha hydrogen radiation, and spectral observations of Earth. The document does not describe any UAP sighting; the content is purely astronomical and astrophysical data analysis from the Apollo 17 instruments.
quotes: When you look in the Milky Way, you see a lot of UV coming from the stars, but the question is, what do you see when you look up to the North Galactic Pole or down to the South Galactic Pole.
The spectrum that we see looks like the spectrum of the hot star; however, we know that there were no hot stars within our field of view.

151.tldr: This is a State Department cable reporting Papua New Guinea's National Intelligence Organization inquiry into unidentified aerial phenomena sightings over PNG on January 24, 1985. Local residents reported fast-moving objects with lights and contrails; an Air Niugini pilot's radar detected aircraft flying south-to-north at high altitude and speed near Angoram, and visual sightings of contrails were reported from multiple locations tracking one aircraft moving north-to-south at 1900 local time and six to eight aircraft moving south-to-north at 2200 local time. The U.S. Embassy confirmed to PNG authorities that no U.S. B-52 overflights or U.S. aircraft were in PNG airspace on that date.

WE HAVE TOLD NIO WE KNEW OF NO B-52 OVERFLIGHTS AND NO U.S. AIRCRAFT IN PNG AIRSPACE ON JANUARY 24

152.tldr: State Department cable reporting a UAP sighting by three American commercial pilots flying a Boeing 747SP over Kazakhstan on January 27, 1994. At 41,000 feet, the crew observed a bright, intensely luminous object approaching from the east at high speed and higher altitude, which maneuvered in circles, corkscrews, and 90-degree turns for approximately 40 minutes before disappearing. The pilots described contrails left by the object at an estimated 100,000 feet altitude and rejected a meteor explanation based on their extensive flying experience; the pilot-in-command, Ed Rhodes, expressed the opinion the object was extraterrestrial and under intelligent control. The State Department transmitted the report with no conclusion.

THEY WATCHED THE OBJECT FOR SOME FORTY MINUTES AS IT MANEUVERED IN CIRCLES, CORKSCREWS AND MADE 90-DEGREE TURNS AT RAPID RATES OF SPEED AND UNDER VERY HIGH G'S.
THERE IS TOO LITTLE AIR/MOISTURE AT THAT EXTREME ALTITUDE TO ENABLE THE CREATION OF CONTRAILS BY THE PROPULSION MECHANISMS OF ORDINARY AIRCRAFT WHICH MIGHT BE ABLE TO REACH THAT HEIGHT.
ON THE BASIS OF ITS SPEED AND MANEUVERABILITY, RHODES EXPRESSED THE OPINION, WHICH HIS CREW SEEMED TO SUPPORT, THAT THE OBJECT WAS EXTRATERRESTRIAL AND UNDER INTELLIGENT CONTROL.

153.tldr: This is a State Department cable from the U.S. Embassy in Moscow, dated October 30, 2001, reporting on Russian denials of airspace violations over Georgia's Kodori Gorge on October 28–29, 2001. Deputy Foreign Minister Mamedov and MFA Georgia Desk Chief Tereoken categorically denied that Russian military aircraft bombed or flew over the region, despite Georgian accusations. Tereoken suggested reports of aircraft "might as well have been about UFOs," implying no aircraft were present. The cable also documents Russian military withdrawal procedures from Gudauta base and notes the ambassador's concern that continued violations could damage U.S.–Russian relations ahead of a presidential summit.

RUSSIAN MINISTRY OF DEFENSE...CATEGORICALLY DENYING THAT RUSSIAN PLANS WERE INVOLVED IN ANY INCIDENTS IN GEORGIAN AIRSPACE
IT IS HARD TO ACCEPT OFFICIAL RUSSIAN DENIALS THAT RUSSIAN PLANES WERE NOT INVOLVED. TO POSIT THAT THEY COULD BE UFOS WOULD BE HUMOROUS IF IT WERE NOT FOR THE SERIOUSNESS OF THE VIOLATIONS.

Location: Kodori Gorge, Abkhazia, Georgia
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mamedov and MFA Georgia Desk Chief Tereoken denied any Russian aircraft involvement
Georgian authorities accused Russian planes of bombing positions in Kodori Gorge
One trainload of Russian military equipment departed Gudauta base and entered Russia on October 29
Approximately 600 Russian personnel remained at Gudauta; Russia insisted on keeping ~340 as "guards"

155.tldr: State Department cable from U.S. Embassy Mexico dated September 16, 2023, reporting on Mexican political developments for the week of September 11–15, 2023. The cable includes a section documenting that on September 12, 2023, the Mexican Congress held a hearing on unidentified aerial phenomena (UAP), featuring testimony from Mexican journalist Jaime Maussan and former U.S. Navy pilot Ryan Graves, who presented alleged alien corpses and pilot encounter videos, with the stated aim of establishing UAP language in Mexico's Aerial Space Protection Law that would make Mexico the first country to formally acknowledge alien life.
quotes: Congress heard testimony on unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) September 12, from experts including from Mexican journalist Jaime Maussan and former U.S. Navy pilot Ryan Graves, who previously testified before the U.S. Congress.
The hearing was to debate language on UAP in the Aerial Space Protection Law which, if approved, would make Mexico the first country to formally acknowledge the presence of alien life on Earth.
Experts also presented to Congress two alleged alien corpses and videos of Mexican pilots' encounters with fast-moving flying objects during flight.
Graves lamented the display took away from his and other pilots' experiences with UAP and expressed disappointment with Maussan's 'unsubstantiated stunt.'

Jaime Maussan (Mexican journalist) and Ryan Graves (former U.S. Navy pilot) provided testimony

Proposed amendment to Aerial Space Protection Law would acknowledge alien life if approved
Scientists previously discredited Maussan's alleged alien corpses

156.tldr: This is an FBI incident report documenting a late 2025 UAP sighting in the United States involving helicopter crews and intelligence officials. On the incident date at approximately 1700–2316 hours, personnel from [OPERATIONS CENTER] conducted an aerial search of a mountain range west of [SITE CODE NAME] following witness reports of orbs/lights and ground impacts. Over a 90-minute window (2202–2257 hours), multiple crews using Forward Looking Infrared, Night Vision Goggles, and naked-eye observation reported sightings of orange orbs with white/yellow centers that flared up and down in formations, moved at high speeds, and appeared to pursue military aircraft in the vicinity. The document contains detailed timeline entries and witness statements but does not provide an explicit conclusion regarding the objects' origin or nature.

160.tldr: This is a continuation page (page 2 of 2) of an FBI FD-302 witness interview form documenting a September 2023 UAP sighting in the United States. The witness observed an object that maintained constant size and light intensity while stationary, which was first noticed as the witness passed through a gate. A second witness was present but unable to view the object. The witness experienced significant psychological effects including disturbed sleep and vivid dreams for two nights following the sighting, and reported a coincidental television outage at their hotel that night.
quotes: The object stayed the same size and kept the same light intensity during the time observed it.
He did not see the object as they were coming over the small bridge at the gate until they were going through the gate.
That night a storm came through and the TV went out in hotel room. He was still freaked out and went downstairs to make sure all the TVs were out in the hotel and not just his.
had weird dreams and had trouble sleeping for the first two nights after he saw the object.

Incident location: United States (specific site near a gated entry)
Object characteristics: constant size and light intensity throughout observation
Witnesses: at least two people present; second witness unable to view object
Post-incident effects: sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, psychological distress lasting minimum two nights
No vehicle interference reported

161.tldr: This is a Department of War incident report documenting multiple unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP) sightings in the western United States in 2023, witnessed by six federal law enforcement special agents across four separate events. Witnesses reported orange orbs launching smaller red orbs, a large glowing orange sphere near a rock formation, a dark kite-shaped object with red and white lights that moved laterally without changing orientation, and a transparent kite-shaped object observed through night vision goggles. The report includes technical measurements by AARO, witness descriptions, and recreated drawings, but does not provide a definitive agency conclusion regarding the nature or origin of the objects.
quotes: Three teams of two federal law enforcement special agents each independently describe seeing orange "orbs" in the sky emit/launch smaller red "orbs" in groups of two to four, with three being the general consensus.
The object didn't change height and appeared to move with "zero resistance." The object stopped about 100 meters off the side of the road and turned off its lights.

USPER5 stated that in the night vision goggles, they could "vaguely see a bright star or two in the distance through the object, though somewhat more faint," leading them to believe the object was somewhat transparent.
The object was described as being "similar to the Eye of Sauron from Lord of the Rings, except without the pupil, or maybe an orange Storm Electrify bowling ball."
key_facts: Incident date: 2023; Location: Western United States
Six federal law enforcement special agents (USPER1–USPER6, plus USPER7) witnessed events over two days at dusk and pre-dawn hours
Orange orb launching red orbs observed at least five times by three independent two-agent teams
Large fiery orange orb near rock pinnacle estimated at 12–18 meters diameter, ~1050 meters from observers, silent, ~1 minute duration
Dark kite-shaped object with red and white lights moved laterally at 15–20 mph with zero resistance; estimated 4 feet wide
Transparent kite-shaped object observed ~6 meters off ground, canted at angle, appeared to float with wind; partially visible through night vision goggles

“Orbs Launching Orbs”
•   Location: Western U.S.
•   Time of Day: Dusk (on two separate days)

•   Three teams of two federal law enforcement special agents each (USPER1 through USPER6) independently
    describe seeing orange “orbs” in the sky emit/launch smaller red “orbs” in groups of two to four, with three
    being the general consensus. This is stated to have occurred at least five times. Each time, the orange orb
    would appear, launch red orbs, then disappear. The orange orb was only visible for one or two seconds. The
    red orbs would generally move away from the orange “mother” orb in a horizontal path, but in a couple of
    instances, one red orb was stated to move “heading up at an angle,” while another witness stated sometimes
    the red orbs would “swoop down” after being launched from the larger orange orb. These events were
    witnessed by multiple teams from varying locations and vantage points over a two-day period. Due to the
    sequential nature of the events, it is not known whether there was a single orange “mother” orb that released
    the groups of red orbs or whether there were multiple orange orbs at play.
 “Large, Fiery Orb”
•   Location: Western U.S.
•   Time of Day: Dusk                                                                           Artist Rendering

•   Two federal law enforcement special agents (USPER5 and USPER6) witness a glowing orange orb at a distance of
    “approximately 500-600 meters,”* where it was perched close to a rock pinnacle. Size was difficult to determine,
    but it appeared to be similar in size to a “small helicopter cockpit.”** Witnesses were unable to clearly see any
    structure other than the glowing orb, though USPER6 noted that the object “did almost appear it might have had a
    small spindle or something connecting it from underneath to the rock formation.” Witnesses stated that the object
    did not emit any noticeable sound. The object was described as being “similar to the Eye or [sic] Sauron from Lord
    of the Rings, except without the pupil, or maybe an orange Storm Electrify bowling ball.”
•   USPER6 stated the object “seemed to be hovering with zero resistance or movement, or to be suspended…” The
    sighting lasted “about a minute.”

* Measurements later gathered by AARO assess the object to have been ~1050 meters away from the observers.
** Measurements later gathered by AARO assess the object to have been between 12-18 meters in diameter.

1.tldr: FBI letter dated September 6, 1966, responding to a citizen inquiry from Mrs. Florence C. Dow of Goffstown, New Hampshire. Dow had written on August 31, 1966, expressing concern that the Amalgamated Flying Saucer Clubs of America (AFSCA) publication she had subscribed to might have communist backing. FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover replied that the Bureau neither evaluates nor draws conclusions about organizations' character or integrity, and noted that Bureau files contained no record of either the correspondent or AFSCA. The document also includes extensive promotional and editorial content from AFSCA's "Flying Saucers International" magazine (Issue #24, July 1966), featuring UFO convention announcements, contactee accounts, and a purported extraterrestrial message.

2.tldr: This is a compilation of FBI memoranda and communications from July–August 1947 documenting early U.S. government investigation into flying disc/saucer reports. It includes multiple witness accounts (Hackensack NJ sighting, August 3, 1947; Midland MI incident, July 10, 1947; Wisconsin airborne sightings) and inter-agency coordination between the FBI, Army Air Forces, and War Department. The FBI's San Francisco office forwarded Army Air Forces investigative reports to the Bureau; the Bureau subsequently conducted its own field interviews and coordinated with military intelligence. In most cases, witnesses provided descriptions of round or disc-shaped objects moving at high speed with no visible propulsion, but no physical evidence or definitive identification was established.
quotes: CASELIA noticed that it was moving too fast to be an ordinary balloon, but he could not discern whether it was globular in form or a disc. He said it was about thirty to forty inches in diameter moving north in a horizontal plane about two hundred yards above the top of the hill.
This flight covered twenty-five (25) miles in fifteen (5) seconds, which is a speed of six thousand (6000) miles per hour.
the object was oval on the top and came to a point on the bottom side... he had no idea where it came from.
DOW AUTHORITIES CONSIDERED STORY FANTASTIC BUT HAVE EXAMINED MATERIAL AND STATE CONTENTS TO BE ORDINARY SAND, NOT RADIO ACTIVE, BUT GIVING OFF AMMONIA GAS
key_facts: Hackensack, NJ sighting: August 3, 1947, ~7:45 PM, round black object 30–40 inches diameter, 200 yards altitude, moving north at high speed
Midland, MI incident: July 10, 1947, ~5:15 PM, white ball 'bushel basket' size near ground, fused sand with ammonia odor recovered
Wisconsin airborne sightings: Two separate observations (1145 and 1430 CST) at ~6000 and 3960 mph respectively, witnessed by Army Air Forces pilots and instructors
FBI received Army Air Forces reports dated July 28, August 4, 1947 from Hamilton Field, Fourth Air Force
Maury Island, WA: Harland Dahl and Fred Crisman reported disc fragments; Capt. Davidson and Lt. Brown died in B-25 crash returning from interview

AUGUST 3, 1947 - MISCELLANEOUS '

Reference is made to tne teletype from the Newark Division
to the Bureau dated August 4, 1947 stating tnat a "Flying Disc" had
been reported to hav¢g been seen at Hackensagk/ New Jersey on August 3
last by one Cotes Russia, UR. and WnLLAARKgRUE.

CHARLES CASELLA, JRk., 287 Euclid Avenue, Hackensack, upon
interview by Special Agent ARTHUR F. WILLIAMS of this Division, stated
that on August 3 he had been standing with WILLIAM TRUEX, a soldier
stationed at Fort Dix, observing a "ham" radio rig atop a two-story
house on Simons Avenue, Hackensack. It was approximately 7:45 pm,
and they were in this vicinity for the purpose of meeting TRUEX's
girlfriend, one JOYCE Me FAKLAND.

TRUEX commented to CASELIA that a child had apparently
lost its balloon. UCASELLA looked and about a block or a halt block
away noticed a round, black object moving from south to north and
east of the stop where he and TRUEX were standing. CASELIA noticed
that it was moving too fast to be an ordinary balloon, but he could
not discern whether it was globular in form or a disc. He said it
was about thirty to forty inches in diameter moving north in a hori-
zontal plane about two hundred yards above the top of the hill at
Summit Avenue and Simons Avenue. It proceeded at a steady rate,
emitted no rays, and was moving fast enougn to require them to turn
their heads steadily in order to follow it. ‘TRUEX's girlfriend came
out about fifteen seconds after they first sighted it. They pointed
it out to her, and she said that it looked like a bird on the horizon
so small. It faded out of sight shortly thereafter. CASELLA said
that a line drawn along its apparent course of flight would go from
the vicinity of Bendix, New Jersey to a point west of Westwood, New
Jersey.

CASELLA also said that a man on the porch across tne street
also noticed it and pointed it out to tne women. CASELIA said that
this man seemed excited but did nothing about it.

CASELLA said tnat he was positive it was no optical illusion.
He was not facing into the sun and saw the object clearly. He also
said tnat he would have thought notning of it except for the speed at
which it was traveling,

Miss JOYCE Mc FARLAND, 476 Simons Avenue, upon interview
by Special Agent WILLIAMS, stated that the event in question occurred
at about 7:30 on tne evening of Sunday, August 3. She said that she
was in the house when CASELIA or IRUEX called to her. She went out
immediately, and they pointed out the object in question. She saw
it just before it disappeared over tne horizon, but she declared that
it was in view from that time for approximately one minute. She said
it was round and silver-blue in color and appeared to be revolving.
She said that she did not recall making any comment that it might have
been a bird and herself had no idea of wnat it could be. In view of
tne distance from which she noticed it, she said tnat it could not
have been more than six inches in diameter but would have been much
larger it she had been near to it. Miss Mc FAXLAND said that sne had
never seen anything like it before.

She said that across tne street the BOOTHS, mother and
daughter, were the only people sitting on tne porcn and she, herself,
did not notice anyone pointing toward the object in question. ‘The
only other person around, to her Imowledge, was GLORIA TRUEX, sister
of WILLIAM TRUEX, who remained in the house and did not see the object
at all.

Mrs. WINFIELD S. BOOTH, 459 Simons Avenue, stated that she
was on the porch on the evening in question with her mother but did
not notice any unusual object in the sky nor had any man been present
there to point out the opject in question.

The following information was received from TRUEX through
interview by Special Agent T. HOWARD WALDRON:

Private WILLIAM A. TRUEX, RA 12282003, Company G, 2nd Bat-
talion, 47tn Infantry Regiment, 9th Division, Fort Dix, New Jersey,
advised he was born April 12, 1930 at Jersey City, New Jersey and
completed eight and one nalf years of school. He enlisted in the
United States Army on May 29, 1947. His mother is Mrs. GRACE FIELDS
of 88 Wales Avenue, River Edge, Bergen County, New Jersey. TRUEX
stated that on Sunday, August 3, 1947, at 8:00 p.m., he was standing
outside tne home of his girlfriend, Miss JOYCE Mc FARLAND, 4/8 Simons
Avenue, Hackensack, New Jersey, accompanied by CHARLES CASELLA of 287
Euclid Avenue, Hackensack, New Jersey, who is his sister's fiance.

He said tnat he and CASELLA were looking at the radio antenna on a
home near the 478 Simons Aveme address wnen they noticed an object
